prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A physician of eminence, some years ago, Was called in, to attend on a lady of fashion, Who had long been admired — and the toast of each beau, Tho’ now, her sunk features excited compassion. The doctor no sooner the lady had eyed, Than he begged, ‘She for once would his freedom forgive If he stepped from the rules of good breeding aside, To mention the terms on which she might live.’ ‘By all means,’ cried the lady, ‘for surely no word A physician may utter, should e’er give offence; Punctilio, in illness, is always absurd, And shows either doctor, or patient wants sense.’ ‘Why then, my dear lady, I cannot resist Pronouncing this truth, like a plain honest man; That if, in the use of white paint you persist No medicine will save you, do all that I can.’ ‘You astonish me, Doctor! but, such is my case, That I may as well die, as leave painting alone; For, should I appear with my natural face Amongst my acquaintance — I should not be known.’

Several years ago, a highly distinguished medical specialist was called to care for a prominent high-society woman. Though she had previously been celebrated as a great beauty sought after by many suitors, her currently gaunt and hollowed appearance now only provoked pity.

As soon as the physician assessed her, he asked for her permission to set aside conventional social etiquette so he could outline the strict conditions necessary to keep her alive.

The woman enthusiastically encouraged him to proceed, remarking that no patient should ever take offense at a healer's words. She noted that clinging to formal manners during a health crisis was foolish and demonstrated an absence of common sense in either the practitioner or the sufferer.

Hearing this, the physician plainly delivered his honest warning: if she refused to stop applying white cosmetics to her skin, no medical intervention within his power would be able to save her life.

Stunned, the lady replied that she might as well face death rather than give up her makeup. She explained that if she were to show her unadorned, natural features to her social circle, no one would even recognize her.

In the quiet luxury of her grand boudoir, an eminent physician was summoned to attend to a lady of high fashion. Once the undisputed belle of society, her celebrated beauty had withered alongside her rapidly deteriorating health. Where vibrant youth and grace had once commanded the admiration of every room, there now lay a fragile figure, plagued by a mysterious and debilitating illness that had ruined her famous appearance and threatened her very life.

After a thorough examination, the physician recognized the true, tragic cause of her decay. Knowing the delicate sensibilities of the aristocratic circle she inhabited, he paused before offering his diagnosis. "Madam," he said with solemn gravity, "if I am to render any true assistance, I must ask your permission to set aside the flattering pleasantries of polite etiquette. The severity of your condition demands that I speak with absolute candor about what you must do if you wish to survive."

The lady, desperate for a cure, offered a weary nod of agreement. She admitted that the rigid rules of social decorum were absurd during a dire medical crisis. Believing herself prepared for any difficult treatment or bitter medicine, she urged the physician to speak freely and withhold nothing.

Taking her at her word, the doctor delivered his stark diagnosis. He plainly informed her that her illness was caused by the very thing she used to conceal it. No potion, tonic, or medical procedure could save her life, he warned, so long as she continued to apply her toxic white face paint. The cosmetic was slowly poisoning her body, and complete abstinence from it was her only hope for recovery.

Upon hearing this, the lady’s resolve shattered, replaced by sheer horror—not at the prospect of dying, but at the thought of being seen without her mask. Confronted with the choice between her life and her vanity, she firmly rejected the doctor's advice. She declared that she would rather embrace the grave than abandon her face paint, bitterly reasoning that if she were to reveal her ruined, natural face, her acquaintances would no longer recognize her at all.
outputs.L4:
The bedchamber of Lady Eleanor Vance was a place designed to deceive time. Curtains of heavy crimson velvet were drawn tight against the afternoon sun, casting the room in a permanent, suffocating twilight. Candles flickered softly, their dim light carefully calibrated to obscure the sharp edges of reality. The air was thick with the suffocating sweetness of lavender oil and dried roses, a desperate attempt to mask the subtle, metallic odor of decay.

For a decade, Lady Eleanor had reigned supreme as the undisputed jewel of London’s high society. Poets praised her porcelain skin, painters begged for her portrait, and noblemen ruined themselves simply to win a smile from her painted lips. But on this overcast autumn morning, it was not an admirer who crossed her threshold, but Dr. Thomas Althorpe, the city’s most eminent physician.

Dr. Althorpe was a man accustomed to the frailties of the human condition, but the figure before him filled him with a profound, solemn dread. Lady Eleanor sat propped against a mound of silk pillows. Even in the gloom, her face possessed a stark, spectral whiteness—smooth, unblemished, and utterly dead. 

"My dear Doctor," she whispered, her voice a raspy shadow of the silvery tones that had once captivated ballrooms. "Tell me you have brought a tincture for my fatigue. I must attend the Duke’s masquerade on Friday, and my legs feel as heavy as lead."

Althorpe set down his leather bag, his expression grim. He walked to the window and, ignoring her soft gasp of protest, pulled back a single curtain. Daylight flooded the room, laying bare the truth.

Up close, the tragedy of Eleanor’s condition was unmistakable. The brilliant white veneer covering her cheeks was not natural; it was Venetian Ceruse—a toxic concoction of white lead and vinegar that she had slathered onto her skin every day for years. Beneath that chalky mask, the insidious poison had done its terrible work. Her gums were swollen and discolored by a telltale blue line. Her limbs trembled with a faint, involuntary palsy, and her eyes, once brilliant, were sunken and yellowed. The very cosmetic she used to hide the fading of her youth was corroding her flesh, rotting her teeth, and failing her internal organs.

With gentle firmness, Dr. Althorpe dampened a linen cloth with warm water and stepped toward her.

"Forgive me, my Lady," he said quietly.

Before she could pull away, he pressed the cloth to her cheek and swept it downward. A swath of the white paste peeled away, revealing the skin beneath—pitted, gray, inflamed, and raw.

Eleanor shrieked, a sound of pure horror, and clutched a silver-handled mirror to her face. She dropped it instantly, the glass shattering on the floor, as if looking at her true self had physically burned her.

"Lady Eleanor, look at me," Dr. Althorpe commanded, taking her trembling, bone-thin hands in his. "I will not offer you sweet lies or useless tonics. You are dying. The white paint you apply every morning is a poison. It is seeping into your blood, failing your heart, and devouring your body from the inside out."

He leaned in closer, his voice cutting through the heavy room with absolute authority. "If you continue to use this ceruse, it will prove fatal before the winter sets in. You must wash your face, throw away those jars, and accept a long, quiet recovery out in the countryside. It is your only chance at survival."

Silence stretched across the room, heavy and suffocating. Eleanor stared at the physician, her breathing shallow and ragged. For a fleeting second, Dr. Althorpe thought he saw a spark of self-preservation in her eyes—a realization of her mortality. 

Then, her gaze drifted to her vanity table. There stood rows of gilded porcelain pots filled with the lethal white paste, flanked by delicate horsehair brushes and rouge pots. 

"Abandon my paint?" she whispered, her lips trembling. A terrifying, frantic laugh escaped her throat. "Doctor, you ask the impossible."

"I ask for your life, Eleanor!" Althorpe insisted, his voice rising in frustration. "Is your breath worth so little to you?"

"My breath is worth nothing if I am invisible!" she cried, a tear cutting a clear, dark path through the white lead on her cheek. "Do you know what society is, Dr. Althorpe? It is a court that grants existence only to the beautiful. If I walk into the Duke’s hall bare-faced, with gray skin and hollow cheeks, they will not pity me. They will recoil. They will whisper. They will forget me while I am still standing in the room."

She pushed his hands away with surprising force, her trembling fingers reaching toward the nearest jar of white ceruse. 

"To be forgotten is a far more painful death than anything this poison can do to me," she murmured, unscrewing the lid with frantic devotion. "If I am to die, I will die as the woman they admired. I will not live as a ghost in their shadows."

Dr. Althorpe stood frozen, paralyzed by the tragic absurdity of her words. He had fought against cholera, consumption, and the bloody aftermath of war, but he had no medicine for a soul so thoroughly infected by vanity and the relentless expectations of a shallow world. He realized with a heavy heart that the lady was already dead; she was merely deciding what costume her corpse would wear.

Without another word, the physician gathered his instruments and closed his leather bag. He gave a final, solemn bow to the tragic figure in the mirror, who was already dipping her brush into the lethal powder, carefully erasing the truth of her mortality, one poison stroke at a time.

Sitting in the corner booth **was** a quiet figure, wrapped in a dark coat, sipping black coffee. Nobody in the small town seemed to know **who** he **was** or where he had come from. He didn't say much to the waitress, **tho** his polite nod and gentle smile made it clear he meant no harm. 

He stayed until the storm passed, staring out the fogged window as if waiting for a signal only he could see. By sunrise, he had vanished as suddenly as he arrived, leaving behind nothing but a generous tip on the table.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 19th-century style rhyming poem about an eminent physician warning a vain high-society lady that her white face paint is poisoning her, but she refuses to give it up because she cares too much about her appearance.
counterfactuals.output:
Upon her velvet stool the lady sat,
Before a mirror framed in carved gilt-wood,
Ignoring grey midnights and shadows that
Besieged the stately chamber where she stood.
With ivory brush she smoothed the deadly cream—
The white ceruse, the heavy paste of lead—
To give her skin a soft, ethereal gleam,
And hide the warm, unworthy blush of red.

Then spake Sir Arthur, grave of eye and brow,
The grand physician of the royal court;
He laid his hand upon her shoulder now,
And checked her hand, and stayed her cruel sport.
"My lady, pause!" the old physician cried,
"This snowy balm you brush upon your cheek
Is steeped in venom, harvested by pride,
To sap the spirit and to break the weak.

"The pale ceruse you deem a flawless grace
Doth seep in secret to your very bone;
It steals the living color from your face,
And turns your tender vitals into stone.
I see the silver shadow on your gum,
The trembling fingers, and the dulling eye!
Abandon this, before the palsies come,
Lest in your youth you lay you down to die."

The Lady Clara turned her slender neck,
And laughed a silver laugh of cold disdain;
She saw no shadow, nor a distant wreck,
Nor heeded she the doctor’s grim refrain.
"Would you have me appear in public sight
With ruddy cheeks, like wenches at the plow?
The ballroom waits! The Duke attends tonight!
They bow before the marble of my brow.

"What care I for the slow and hidden blight,
If I may reign supreme above the crowd?
I’d rather shine, the blossom of a night,
Than wear a healthy face beneath a shroud!
To lose my bloom is worse than any grave,
To feel the touch of wrinkles on my skin;
If beauty be the price that I must pay,
I’ll buy the mask, and let the poison in."

She raised the brush, and dipped it in the shell,
And smoothed again the fatal, chalky glaze;
Sir Arthur sighed, a sad and mute farewell,
And left her to her brief and blinded days.

And in the glass, a ghastly spectre shone—
A painted corpse adorned in pearls and thread,
Who traded life to sit upon a throne,
Already numbered with the silent dead.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a humorous ballad illustrating the idea that some people would literally rather die than go out in public without makeup.
counterfactuals.output:
Come gather, friends, and hear the tale
Of Lady Bella Vance,
Who’d never step beyond her door
And leave her face to chance.

No mortal eye had seen her pores,
No soul had seen her skin;
To show a blemish to the world
She deemed a mortal sin.

She’d paint a jawline where was none,
And glue an eyelash high,
She’d rather face a firing squad
Than go out high and dry.

One fateful Tuesday afternoon,
A terrible event!
The toaster sparked, the curtains blazed,
The smoke alarm was spent!

The kitchen burned, the hallway choked
With fumes of thickest black!
The neighbors fled into the street
With coats upon their back.

Brave Fireman Bob burst through the door,
"Miss! You must evacuate!"
She shrieked and covered up her cheeks,
"Step back! You’ll have to wait!

Where is my shade of 'Nude Desire'?
Where is my setting spray?
If I go out bare-faced right now,
What will the neighbors say?"

"The roof is falling!" cried the man,
"The floor is burning hot!"
She hissed, "My eyebrows aren't drawn on,
I’m stepping out... I'm NOT!

Without my contour, I possess
No jawline of my own!
My under-eyes are dark as night,
I look like skin and bone!

I have no blush! I have no bronze!
My T-zone’s full of shine!
To be exposed in natural light
Is where I draw the line!"

He tried to scoop her in his arms,
To drag her down the stairs,
She fought him off with desperate strength,
Ignoring all his prayers.

"No camera crew shall catch my forehead!
No TikTok film my dread!
If I must be seen un-concealed,
I’d rather end up dead!"

She dove back into the inferno,
Ignoring heat and flame,
To search the ashes for a mascara,
To save her public name.

They found her in the smoldering ruins,
A monument to pride—
A tube of red lipstick in her hand,
The moment that she died.

So lay her down in velvet dark,
With foundation thick and grand,
And blend it smoothly to the neck,
With a gentle, loving hand.

And place a mirror in her casket,
Adjust her halo’s light—
Lest in the grave her ghost should wake
And not look photo-right!
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an 18th-century medical satire poem about lead face paint.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Saturnine Seductress;**
*or, The Lady’s Fatal Paste*

When fair Clarissa seeks the courtly plain,
And strives to conquer every foolish swain,
She scorns the blush that simple Health bestows,
And craves a skin more pale than Alpine snows.
Behold her glass! Where eager Vanity
Consults the deadly arts of Alchemy:
She seeks no bloom of modest, natural grace,
But coats with toxic dust her morning face.

With fine *Ceruse*—the heavy crust of Lead—
She smears the living skin to match the dead;
Steeped in sharp vinegar, the metal bleeds
A corpse-like balm to serve her beauty’s needs.
What though it hides the scars of poxes past?
This alabaster bloom is built to last!

"Buy, Ladies, buy!" the cunning Quack proclaims,
"The sovereign salve for high-born courtly dames!
It smooths the brow, it whitens every spot,
And cures the cheek of any earthly rot!"
He sells the jar, then chuckles in his sleeve,
To see how easily the fair deceive;
For while he vows it drives all age away,
It speeds his client to her native clay.

Now Saturn enters through the porous skin,
And works his quiet tragedy within.
A charming *palsy* shakes her slender wrist;
Her wretched bowels by *colic* twinges twist;
Her pearly teeth turn black as sea-coal fires,
And drop like withered leaves as youth expires;
Her breath grows sweet with pestilential fumes,
While Saturn’s rust her nervous strength consumes.

Yet still she paints! And as the vapors rise,
A fashionable frenzy lights her eyes.
The gallants sigh, "Observe her ghost-like grace!
No vulgar blood pollutes that porcelain face!"
Indeed, no blood—for Lead has claimed the whole,
Paralyzed her limbs, and wrecked her soul.

At last the Doctor comes with solemn tread,
To write a Latin cure for one that’s dead.
He blames the *Humors*, or the chilly air,
And charges twenty guineas for his care;
He shakes his wig, declares her *Vapors* foul,
While through the drapes the mournful night-winds howl.
No undertaker needs her cheek to bleach—
She reached the pallor that the fashions preach.

**THE MORAL**

Ye British Belles, attend this ghastly tale,
Nor strive by Poison’s aid to grow so pale;
Let rosy Health your native cheeks adorn,
And leave the Lead for roofs and pipes unborn.
For she who paints with Saturn’s heavy dust,
Exchanges fickle Youth for graveyard rust—
And striving for the hue of Angels tread,
Saves work for Undertakers when she’s dead!
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
